name: Damu
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. 2011. Prosody and typological drift in Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman. In Mon-Khmer Studies Special Issue 3 (ICAAL4 vol. 2), 198-221.
sources.note: Family-level only: 'all known Tani languages appear to exhibit a falling rhythm', trochaic effects weakest in Eastern Tani, strongest in Upper Belt Nyishi; Damu not named or described.

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. 2015. Tones in Northeast Indian languages, with a focus on Tani: a fieldworker's guide. In Post, Morey & DeLancey (eds.), Language and Culture in Northeast India and Beyond: In Honor of Robbins Burling (Asia-Pacific Linguistics 023), 182-210. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: p.190: 'Little or nothing is known about the remaining known Tani lects, i.e. Bokar-Ramo, Pailibo, Hill Miri, Bori, Aashing, Shimong and Damu'; Table 5 lists Damu under 'Unknown' for tone; fn.5: 'Ou-Yang (1985) claimed that none of the Bengni, Bokar or Damu lects that he recorded in Tibet had tone... Ou-Yang's further claim that Bokar and Damu lack tone should not be taken as definitive.' Nothing on stress in Damu.

sources.citation: Sun, T.-S. Jackson. 2003. Tani languages. In Thurgood & LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages (1st ed.), 456-466. London: Routledge (archive.org djvu excerpt).
sources.note: Mentions Damu only as transitional/difficult to subclassify and as having 'as many as ten vowels (Ouyang 1985: 77)'; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Namkung, Ju (ed.). 1996. Phonological Inventories of Tibeto-Burman Languages (STEDT Monograph 3). Berkeley. Entry 'DAMU' pp.86-87 (inventory from J. Sun 1993a pp.497-498 < Ouyang 1985).
sources.note: Segmental inventory only (initials, rhymes; vowel length contrastive only in open syllables); no tone or stress information.

sources.citation: Sun, Jackson T.-S. 1993. The linguistic position of Tani (Mirish) in Tibeto-Burman: a lexical assessment. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(2): 143-188.
sources.note: Lexical subgrouping paper; no phonological description of Damu; nothing on stress (pp.1-6 scanned and read; remainder is cognate comparison).

sources.citation: Sun, Tianshin Jackson. 1993. A Historical-Comparative Study of the Tani (Mirish) Branch in Tibeto-Burman. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (2007 re-typeset PDF, 471 pp., from Wayback copy of ling.sinica.edu.tw).
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: hathitrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: Appendix II 'Damu OY' (PDF p.447-448 = printed 438-439): onset/rhyme inventory, 'Vowel length is distinct only in open syllables', '(4) Tonality: Damu is not a tone language.' Appendix I (PDF p.426 = printed 417): 'a heavily Tibetanized variety of Tani... Damu is not a tone language.' p.20: Ouyang observed 'Bokar, Damu and Bengni do not have contrastive tones'. Data second-hand from Ouyang 1985. Nothing on word stress/accent placement anywhere (suprasegmentals treated = length + tonality only).
States: 'No documentation or description of the Damu language other than some brief remarks and a word list in Ouyang (1985) appears to exist.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Post, Mark W. & Jackson T.-S. Sun. 2017. Tani languages. In G. Thurgood & R. LaPolla (eds.), The Sino-Tibetan Languages, 2nd ed., 322-337. London: Routledge.

sources.note: Most recent family survey by the two Tani specialists; phonology section covers tone/word prosody across Tani and mentions Damu; would state what is known of Damu prosody.

sources.citation: Ouyang Jueya 欧阳觉亚. 1985. 珞巴族语言简志(崩尼—博嘎尔语) Luobazu yuyan jianzhi (Bengni-Boga'er yu). Beijing: Minzu chubanshe. '方言' chapter pp.76-121 (Damu section from p.77); also the Bokar 语音 chapter for any 重音 remark. (Reprinted in 中国少数民族语言简志丛书 修订本, 2009.)

sources.note: The only first-hand description of Damu (phonemic inventory, remarks, wordlist from 1976 fieldwork); if any statement on Damu stress/重音 exists it is here.

sources.note: Full grammar of Tangam, Damu's closest relative (Glottolog Damu-Tangam node); its introduction discusses Damu and its phonology chapter describes tone and word prosody for the sister language.
